key_insight: The paper shows that in recursive state estimation, making each local solver more exact does not always improve the final outcome. It characterizes when an approximate correction can still be acceptable within a tolerance and how solver defects influence the covariance over time.
problem_solved: It addresses the challenge of using inexact or approximate numerical solvers inside feedback-based state estimation systems, where local approximation errors can accumulate and affect overall filter reliability.
method: Analyzes a fixed linear Kalman filtering setting to define when a correction is admissible under a chosen subspace and norm budget.
Studies how the actually executed solver defects propagate through the filter and shape finite-horizon covariance behavior.
Centers each defect relative to the exact gain for the implemented covariance to isolate and measure the impact of approximation errors.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners building real-time estimation systems, this work helps determine when approximate computations are safe and how much solver inexactness can be tolerated. It provides guidance for balancing speed, robustness, and accuracy in hardware-constrained or resource-limited deployments.
visual_elements: A feedback-loop diagram of recursive state estimation with an approximate solver block highlighted.
A side-by-side comparison of exact vs. inexact gain updates and their effect on covariance.
A tolerance/budget diagram showing admissible correction regions in a subspace.
A time-series chart showing covariance response across finite horizons under different defect levels.
paper_title: Repairability of Inexact Solvers in Recursive State Estimation with Machine Learning
paper_authors: Yanjun Ji, Dennis Willsch, Orkun Şensebat, Priyanka Arkalgud Ganeshamurthy, Zhi Pei
